Annex 4 AAP in donor proposals
Given that AAP commitments and responsibilities are embedded in the humanitarian architecture, 
donors expect AAP approaches to be embedded in proposals for emergency funding. WHO should 
seek to reflect any of the AAP approaches and activities that are planned or already implemented in all 
emergency donor proposals. The below gives an outline of the type of information donors will expect 
to see.
Project rationale/justification/needs assessment/needs analysis
 • Describe consultations undertaken with affected people to ensure their participation in identifying 
the priority needs to be addressed by the programme. This should include the number of people 
consulted, who was consulted (disaggregated by sex, age, disability and location), how these 
consultations were designed to be inclusive of the most marginalized, and a summary of their 
priority needs and inputs into programme design.
 • Describe any other data sources used to understand needs that reflect the voices of affected people, 
for example, beneficiary monitoring data from previous programmes or complaints and feedback 
data. Provide numbers/percentages of people expressing certain needs disaggregated by sex, age, 
disability and location.
 • Describe the differing needs of different groups of people, and back these up with data.
 • Describe affected people’s communication, information and participation preferences. 
Project activities 
 • Describe how the programme design has been adapted to meet the expressed needs, priorities and 
preferences of affected people.
 • Describe plans for the ongoing participation of affected people in decision-making throughout the 
programme and what tools and mechanisms will be used, for example, participatory monitoring, 
community committees, CFMs etc.
 • Describe information provision activities planned, mechanisms to be used, key messages that 
will be shared and any adaptations that will be made to ensure these activities reach the most 
vulnerable people, including people with specific needs.
 • Describe the CFM in place, adaptations made to ensure the CFM is accessible for vulnerable people 
and people with specific needs, and processes in place for issue referral and closure, including 
for sensitive complaints. Describe how complaints and feedback data will be used to feed into 
programme decision-making.

advisable to have at least one to two AAP indicators in all the above.

a baseline and regular progress values. The data collection mechanisms can be implemented directly 
by WHO or by implementing partners.

Annex 7 Immediate AAP activities for a sudden 
onset emergency
The list of actions below is for use by country offices who may not have established any AAP activities 
and processes prior to the start of a crisis.
1. Assign and orient AAP/community engagement focal points for WHO and for the health cluster, 
with responsibility for promoting and leading all AAP/community engagement and accountability 
discussion and activities in the initial response, outlined in the points below.
2. Ensure community engagement and feedback is on the agenda of all operational meetings within 
WHO and the health cluster.
3. Instruct partners, including ministry of health, on minimum questions to determine community 
needs.
4. Collect, collate and share information from partner reports on community needs, that is, answers to 
the above questions, either in rapid needs assessment or through ad hoc key informant interviews 
with leaders of community organizations. 
5. Coordinate and share information for communities (FAQ, service availability, contact information 
including any numbers to report SEA).
6. Be in touch with other UN agencies, international NGOs or AAP working groups regarding any 
existing or planned CFMs that will be used for the initial response, or any coordinated plans to 
establish one. Ensure WHO and health partner participation in collaborative CFM efforts.
7. Coordinate and implement initial community consultations through partners and ministry of health 
(ensure inclusive approach to cover needs of different groups).

Annex 8 AAP in PHSA
Table A8.1 describes the AAP information to be included in different sections of the PHSA document.
Note on source data:
 • Where possible, use secondary data sources that have engaged with different vulnerable groups 
of affected people and reflect their perspectives on their immediate and long-term needs and 
priorities.
 • These data sources could include complaints and feedback data from existing CFMs (WHO, partner 
or collective mechanisms); community consultation data; focus group discussion data; needs 
assessment; and monitoring or evaluation data that reflects the expressed views of different groups 
of affected people. Some qualitative data sources should be used.
Table A8.1 AAP in PHSA document
PHSA section What to include
Health status 
and threats/
humanitarian 
profile
State what participatory data was used and which population groups’ 
perspectives are represented. 
Identify vulnerable groups within the given context: groups that may be 
specifically vulnerable to certain health threats and groups that may be 
vulnerable as a result of societal norms, power structures or mobility issues 
that prevent them from accessing the health care they require (e.g. children, 
women and girls, people with disabilities, displaced and stateless people, 
refugees, elderly, religious or ethnic minorities, LGBTIQ+ people). 
Health system 
status and local 
health system 
disruptions
This should consider the perspectives of affected people. For example, CFM 
data could be used to understand health system status and disruptions 
as reported by affected people. There may be disruptions that are best 
identified by affected people and communities, community organizations, 
community leaders and local and national actors.
Humanitarian 
health response
Participation and inclusion: reflect successful strategies and methodologies 
used by WHO, the ministry of health or health partners to involve 
communities in health-related decision-making, and the extent to which 
these have been successful at engaging the most marginalized or how they 
could be adapted to do so.
Information provision and transparency: reflect any successful public health 
communication strategies already in place by partners, and the extent to 
which these have reached the most marginalized groups and could be used 
to communicate AAP and PSEA messages to affected people. 
Complaints and feedback: reflect information on existing CFM (including for 
PSEA), if these are accessible to the vulnerable and at-risk groups in need of 
assistance and can receive and refer health-related issues.
Information gaps 
and information 
source
Where any of the above information or data sources are missing from the 
PHSA, these should be identified as gaps in knowledge that need to be filled.
CFM: complaints and feedback mechanism; LGBTIQ+: lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, intersex or 
queer; PHSA: public health situation analysis; PSEA: protection from sexual exploitation and abuse.

Annex 11 AAP activities at different stages of the 
AAP journey
Tables A11.1 to A11.3 show the different activities that should be implemented across the pillars of 
participation and inclusion, information and transparency, and complaints and feedback at different 
stages of a country office’s implementation of AAP processes.
Table A11.1 Start of AAP journey
Pillar AAP activities
Participation 
and inclusion
 • Map existing community consultation platforms and methods being 
used for health programmes (within WHO, under the ministry of health 
or by other humanitarian health partners). Assess whether these ensure 
representation from the most vulnerable and isolated, whether they 
can be adapted to do so, or whether new platforms and methods are 
needed. 
 • Speak to affected people to understand their needs and preferences 
when it comes to participating in decision-making on WHO’s 
programmes. Understand their opinion on existing and possible new 
platforms and methods. Make sure this information is collected from 
the most vulnerable groups to plan for any adaptations to ensure 
accessibility.
 • Select the best platforms and methodologies for WHO to use to ensure 
the participation of affected people in decision-making. Decide how 
these will be implemented to overcome barriers to the involvement of 
vulnerable groups.
 • Map upcoming opportunities in programmes when key decisions will 
be made and when the participation of affected people is important. 
Schedule these in workplans. These should include opportunities across 
the programme cycle. Decide what level of participation you are aiming 
for in each of these opportunities. 
 • Anticipate what organizational barriers may hinder the participatory 
process for each of these opportunities, and ensure solutions are 
considered at this stage. 
 • Identify organizational decision-making spaces, such as operational 
meetings and senior management meetings, where the voices of 
affected people need to be reflected in decisions.

Pillar AAP activities
Information 
and 
transparency
 • Understand the communication context.
 • Map the existing communication channels used by WHO, the ministry 
of health or other health partners to provide information to affected 
people. Understand which are the most effective and whether they 
reach the most vulnerable and isolated. 
 • Speak to affected people to understand their needs and preferences 
when it comes to the type of information they need and the way 
they would prefer to receive it. Understand their opinion on existing 
and possible new channels for providing information. Make sure this 
information is collected from the most vulnerable groups to plan for any 
adaptations to ensure accessibility.
 • Map opportunities to provide information to affected people that exist 
within programmes, for example where there is already face-to-face 
contact between affected people and WHO/partner staff or health 
workers, or where existing health messaging is being delivered and there 
is an opportunity to add to this.
 • Using the above, select the best communication channels for WHO 
to use to ensure information provision and transparency for affected 
people. 
 • Decide on the areas of information that need to be detailed and 
delivered going forward.
Complaints and 
feedback
 • Understand/map existing interagency or health-related CFMs. 
 • Understand if they meet WHO’s requirements.
 • Speak to affected people to understand their needs and preferences 
when it comes to providing feedback and making a complaint. 
Understand their opinion on existing and possible new channels for a 
CFM. Make sure this information is collected from the most vulnerable 
groups to plan for any adaptations to ensure accessibility.
 • Decide whether WHO will join an existing CFM, or if it is better for WHO to 
establish its own mechanism. 
 • If establishing a new CFM, at a minimum WHO should be able to receive, 
process and close relevant health referrals from existing mechanisms.
AAP: accountability to affected people; CFM: complaints and feedback mechanism.

Table A11.2 Putting AAP systems in place
Pillar AAP activities
Participation and 
inclusion
 • Decide which participatory platform or methodology will be used for 
each identified opportunity for the input of affected people in decision-
making.
 • Prepare to implement each participatory process by:
 – ensuring appropriate gender balance of staff undertaking these 
activities
 – training staff on participatory approaches
 – preparing key information for affected people in accessible formats
 – ensuring adaptations are in place to support the involvement of 
vulnerable groups
 – outlining questions needing answers or areas requiring input
 – deciding the best methodology for each opportunity.
 • Reassess organizational barriers for that area, and prepare for how 
these will be handled during the session.
 • Implement participatory processes and document affected people’s 
views and perspectives. 
 • Feed perspectives of affected people into programme decision-
making spaces and processes. Ensure all perspectives are considered 
and addressed. If some ideas will be implemented, set a time frame 
for doing so. If some ideas cannot be implemented, document the 
reasons why.
 • Include information on adaptations to information provision and 
transparency activities made or not made, so that this is reported back 
to affected people.
 • Report on these processes, who and how many people participated 
and the resulting programme adaptations in WHO internal reports and 
donor reports.
 • Make sure that programme staff are regularly visiting affected 
communities to hear directly from them about their needs and 
experiences of WHO programmes and adaptations.

Document 74
Source: D:\Fobes Internship\RAG-Project\data\Accountability to Affected People Handbook.pdf

Characters: 2590
================================================================================

Pillar AAP activities
Information and 
transparency
 • Draft AAP messages under each of the previously determined areas of 
information. Start with an FAQ document directed at affected people 
to form the basis of information to be provided. This can be based on 
frequent questions coming from affected people, plus key information 
on WHO health programmes and their rights, including PSEA. The FAQ 
can be the basis for all beneficiary messaging and can be adapted to 
suit different methods of communication.
 • Translate the FAQ into local languages. Test the content and language 
with affected people for comprehension and to identify areas for 
improvement. Implement these improvements. Make sure to align 
terminology among health partners and develop a shared FAQ at 
health sector level if possible.
 • Train beneficiary-facing staff on the FAQ document and provide them 
with a copy. Make sure that this document forms the basis for verbal 
information provided to affected people to ensure accuracy and 
consistency.
 • Draft a communication plan that outlines the different channels 
and messaging to be used for each programme area. Make sure that 
adaptations are made to ensure communication reaches the most 
vulnerable and isolated.
 • Implement the communication plan. 
Complaints and 
feedback
 • Ensure all CFM requirements are in place before launching the CFM.
 • Launch the CFM through a community awareness campaign. This 
should be done even if WHO is joining an existing mechanism, to make 
sure WHO-targeted communities are aware of the CFM and how to 
access it.
 • Follow SOPs in place to ensure that the full feedback loop is addressed, 
including ensuring that all issues are closed on an individual level.
 • Keep a close eye on internal referral and closure processes to make 
sure that staff with these responsibilities are following SOPs. Make any 
adjustments needed to SOPs and roles and responsibilities. 
 • Ensure that newly arising FAQs feed into updating the FAQ document.
 • Regularly analyse data to understand trends in different locations, and 
include unusual outliers.
 • Make sure this data is shared with operational teams and senior 
management in spaces where it can be discussed, and corrective 
action agreed, documented and followed up on.
AAP: accountability to affected people; CFM: complaints and feedback mechanism; FAQs: frequently 
asked questions; PSEA: protection from sexual exploitation and abuse; SOPs: standard operating 
procedures.

Table A11.3 Learning, adapting and improving your AAP
Pillar AAP activities
Participation and 
inclusion
 • Adapt participatory approaches to changing programmes and 
operational areas. 
 • Monitor affected people’s satisfaction with processes of participation. 
Understand how they think this could be improved and implement 
these improvements.
 • Monitor affected people’s satisfaction with their level of involvement 
in programme decision-making and with the extent their views and 
opinions are being considered. Understand how they think this could 
be improved, and implement these improvements.
 • Assess the levels of participation of the most vulnerable groups across 
participatory approaches and understand if there are differences 
in their levels of satisfaction with these processes and their results. 
Understand how they think these could be improved and implement 
these improvements.
 • Review the level of participation WHO is aiming for across different 
programmatic decisions and plan to increase the level where feasible.
 • Review the extent to which the voices of affected people are feeding 
effectively into WHO decision-making spaces and if any changes or 
adaptations are needed to ensure that this improves.
Information and 
transparency
 • Monitor affected people’s knowledge and understanding of key 
programme information (e.g. how to access health services/
information, eligibility criteria, how to make a complaint etc.). 
 • Assess the levels of knowledge and understanding of the most 
vulnerable groups and understand if there are differences for different 
groups. Understand how they think this could be improved in your 
communication strategy and implement these improvements.
 • Hear from affected people the best way to improve their knowledge 
and understanding and implement these changes.
 • Review and update the beneficiary-focused FAQ to reflect programme 
changes and to ensure transparency in information provided.
Complaints and 
feedback
 • Monitor the CFM to understand coverage and accessibility, by 
disaggregating data by user demographics and including CFM 
monitoring questions in regular monitoring tools (or establishing 
new tools where no regular monitoring tools exist). Identify areas for 
improvement and understand perspectives of communities on how to 
make improvements. Implement these improvements.
 • Review the CFM closure rate and identify challenges and delays with 
processes. Identify and implement solutions/improvements.
 • Monitor the satisfaction of affected people with the CFM, and the 
way that issues are addressed. Identify areas for improvement 
and understand perspectives of communities on how to make 
improvements. Implement these improvements.
 • Review the extent to which CFM data is feeding effectively into WHO 
decision-making spaces and whether any changes or adaptations are 
needed to ensure this improves.
AAP: accountability to affected people; CFM: complaints and feedback mechanism.

Dr Mike Ryan
Executive Director Health Emergencies Programme/Deputy Director General WHO
Foreword 
“The right to participate is an essential feature of the right to the 
highest attainable standard of health. People have the right and 
duty to participate individually and collectively in the planning and 
implementation of their health and wellbeing.” (1)
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General, World Health Organization
As of December 2024, the World Health Organization (WHO) was responding to 17 acute and protected 
emergencies requiring the highest level of support (G3 and P3), out of a total of 42 emergencies that 
the organization was responding to. It is estimated that 305 million people will require humanitarian 
assistance in 2025 (2). In an ever-changing world fraught with complex emergencies, WHO’s role in 
responding to health crises has never been more critical. At the heart of these efforts lie the individuals, 
communities and populations directly impacted by such emergencies. Affected communities are the 
experts on their health needs and priorities. They are the first to respond to family and community 
needs when a crisis hits. They understand what works and what does not work. To deliver effective 
humanitarian health responses, WHO must also harness and act on this knowledge and capacity, in 
conjunction with evidence and scientific facts, and put people affected by crisis at the centre of our 
responses.
Implementing humanitarian responses that are accountable to affected people means empowering 
people with information, opportunities to express their needs and to take an active part in decision-
making. It is about being inclusive and encouraging the participation of the most vulnerable in 
communities and contributes considerably to community health protection. Most importantly it 
is about WHO being answerable to affected people by responding to their queries and feedback, 
informing them of progress and setbacks, and seeking out and acting on their ideas. 
This approach is embedded in WHO’s constitution (3), which outlines that “Informed opinion and 
active co-operation on the part of the public are of the utmost importance in the improvement of 
the health of the people.” They are also a key feature of the community protection component in the 
health emergency prevention, preparedness, response and resilience (HEPR) framework (4), which 
states that “communities must be at the centre of efforts to prepare for, prevent and respond to health 
emergencies. … interventions must be co-created with affected communities” . 
Prioritizing accountability to affected people (AAP) in WHO’s emergency responses is not only an ethical 
imperative, but also a strategic choice that will lead to more effective interventions and safer and better 
protected communities throughout the emergency management cycle. Principals have committed to 
it, and WHO is determined to further operationalize this approach in emergency response operations 
under its Emergency response framework, edition 2.1 (5). The benefits of implementing such an 
approach are clear, and the time to scale up action is now. As we strive to build a healthier world, let us 
ensure that the voices of those we serve remain at the centre of our efforts.

The AAP Handbook was written by Sara Fowler, AAP consultant, under the direction and supervision of 
Adelheid Marschang, Senior Emergency Officer in the Fragile, Conflict-Affected and Vulnerable Settings 
team, WHO Health Emergencies Programme.

Finally, WHO would like to thank NORAD, the Norwegian Agency for Development Cooperation, for 
funding the development of this Handbook.
How the Handbook was developed
This is the first WHO guidance that supports the integration of AAP in WHO’s Health Emergencies 
Programme (WHE) operations. It should be used together with the Global Health Cluster AAP – 
operational guidance (6) and Minimum standards – AAP (7) which guide health partners in the 
implementation of AAP .
The following process was followed: 
 • desk review of existing and upcoming global commitments and standards that relate to AAP as well 
as other agency-specific guidance on implementing AAP;
 • key informant interviews with knowledgeable stakeholders and end users within WHO;
 • presentation of draft Handbook to WHO headquarters, regional and country-level audiences for 
internal peer review; and
 • external peer review of the Handbook.

Glossary
Accountability to affected people (AAP)
An active commitment to use power responsibly by taking account of, giving account to, and being 
held to account by the people humanitarian organizations seek to assist.
Affected people 
Affected people are all the people in a context where their lives are directly or indirectly impacted by 
conflict, disaster or crisis. 
Complaint 
A complaint is a piece of feedback from someone who is objecting to the actions of an organization or 
its staff because they are unfair, unacceptable or not meeting expected standards and commitments.
Community engagement 
The collaborative process that involves people in assessing their needs and in developing programmes 
that are acceptable and workable for them. The goal is to empower communities to develop shared 
leadership throughout the emergency response cycle.
Diversity
Diversity is the range of human differences, including gender, gender identity, age, nationality, ethnic 
background, beliefs, sexual orientation, ability or other characteristics. These characteristics will lead 
people to have different experiences, needs and vulnerabilities in humanitarian contexts.
Feedback
Feedback is a positive, negative or neutral opinion shared with an organization regarding its 
programmes, way of operating or the behaviour of its staff. Organizations may solicit feedback by 
proactively asking people for their opinions, or receive unsolicited feedback when someone chooses 
to approach the organization and provide their opinion.
Inclusion
Inclusion is the practice of providing equal access to opportunities, resources and rights for people 
who might otherwise be marginalized or excluded, such as minority groups. 
Participation
Participation is people’s active involvement and engagement in the decision-making and activities of 
humanitarian organizations. It is important that all people have equal access to participate, so that 
their views and opinions are reflected in decision-making. 
Protection from sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA)
PSEA is the package of measures taken by organizations to prevent and respond to sexual exploitation 
and abuse (SEA) of affected people by humanitarian staff. These measures aim to ensure affected 
people understand the expected conduct of staff and have access to safe and confidential reporting 
channels. SEA allegations are investigated and acted upon by organizations, and SEA survivors are 
provided with the required support. 
Risk communication
Risk communication is the real-time exchange of information, advice and opinions between experts 
and officials and people who are facing a threat to their health, survival, or economic or social well-
being. The goal of risk communication is to help people make informed decisions and take protective 
actions to mitigate the effects of the threat. 
Sexual exploitation and abuse (SEA)
Sexual exploitation is any actual or attempted abuse of a position of vulnerability, differential power 
or trust for sexual purposes. It includes, but is not limited to, profiting monetarily, socially or politically 
from the sexual exploitation of another. Sexual abuse is the actual or threatened physical intrusion of 
a sexual nature, whether by force or under unequal or coercive conditions. SEA by humanitarian staff  
against affected people they serve represents one of the most serious breaches of accountability.

Chapter 1  
Introduction
1.1 About this Handbook
1.1.1 Purpose
This Handbook was designed to support WHO Health Emergencies Programme (WHE) staff to put 
people affected by humanitarian crises at the centre of decision-making on emergency health 
responses, and to guide WHE staff in operationalizing WHO’s commitments to accountability to 
affected people (AAP). This will enable WHO to meet the needs of affected people in a way that 
makes sense for them, that utilizes their existing capacities and strengthens their resilience in the 
long term. 
By making sure that affected communities play an active role in decisions that affect the provision 
of humanitarian health assistance, we are ensuring higher quality and more effective outcomes that 
preserve the dignity of those we serve.
1.1.2 Audience
This Handbook is for country office, regional and headquarters WHE staff and other people who 
support country operations. The Handbook details AAP responsibilities across the emergency response 
framework (ERF) critical functions. All WHE teams must refer to it at all stages of the programme cycle 
and when drafting key response documentation. 
1.1.3 Use
The Handbook is divided into eight chapters: 
 • Chapter 1 Introduction: overview of the Handbook and AAP , WHO’s global AAP commitments and 
community engagement; 
 • Chapter 2 WHO’s AAP principles;
 • Chapter 3 AAP in WHO’s emergency response framework: AAP responsibilities across the seven 
critical functions, signposts to relevant Handbook sections, and progress indicators;
 • Chapter 4 AAP in the humanitarian programme cycle: minimum actions to integrate AAP across the 
programme cycle;
 • Chapter 5 Participation and inclusion: minimum actions to ensure participation and inclusion of 
affected people in decision-making;
 • Chapter 6 Information provision and transparency: minimum actions in providing adequate 
information and ensuring transparency for affected people; 
 • Chapter 7 Complaints and feedback: minimum actions to ensure that WHO receives and responds 
to feedback from affected people, and programmes are adapted accordingly; and 
 • Chapter 8 Partnerships, collective AAP and coordination: considerations when implementing AAP 
through and with government and nongovernmental organization (NGO) partners.

Resources are highlighted throughout the Handbook. The 11 annexes contain example templates, 
terms of reference, and content for needs assessments, operational plans, logframes, donor proposals 
and more.
This Handbook should be used to inform acute and protracted emergency response programmes 
directly implemented by WHO teams in country, through partnership with the health ministry, the health 
cluster and/or other implementing partners. Although this Handbook is aimed at WHO emergency 
operations, the concepts and ideas within are relevant across the humanitarian–development–peace 
nexus and should be used to influence all WHO programming.
1.2 What is AAP? 
The Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) defines AAP as “an active commitment to use power 
responsibly by taking account of, giving account to, and being held to account by the people 
humanitarian organisations seek to assist.” (8)

1.2.1 A rights-based approach
AAP is founded on a rights-based approach that values affected people as rights holders who should 
be empowered to know and claim their rights and participate in decisions that impact their lives. 
WHO is a duty bearer. In implementing its AAP commitments, WHO increases its accountability for 
respecting, protecting and fulfilling the rights of affected people.
All WHO Member States have ratified at least one international human rights treaty that includes the 
right to the highest attainable standard of health (9).  To deliver on these commitments, countries 
must mainstream fundamental human rights principles and standards in public health emergency 
preparation and response. These principles include:
 • non-discrimination and equality: prioritizing the needs of those furthest behind to achieve equity;
 • participation: empowering health service users and communities to engage in planning, decision-
making and implementation processes for health across the programme cycle and at all levels of 
the system; and
 • accountability: the requirement for countries to establish accessible and effective accountability 
(10).
Actively implementing these principles is key to achieving humanitarian health responses that are 
accountable to affected people. 
1.3 Global commitments on AAP 
The humanitarian sector has developed global commitments to assist agencies in ensuring their 
programming is more effective and accountable. 
1.3.1 IASC
The IASC is the highest level humanitarian coordination forum  of the United Nations system. It 
brings together the executive heads of 19 organizations and consortia, including WHO, to formulate 
policy, set strategic priorities and mobilize resources in response to humanitarian crises. In November 
2017, the IASC Principals endorsed the following four Commitments (11) on AAP and protection from 
sexual exploitation and abuse (PSEA) (Fig. 2).
Fig. 2 IASC revised commitments on AAP and PSEA
Leadership Demonstrate their commitment to Accountability to Affected Populations 
(AAP) and Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) by enforcing, 
institutionalising and integrating AAP approaches in the Humanitarian Program 
Cycle and strategic planning processes, at country level and by establishing 
appropriate management systems to solicit, hear and act upon the voices and 
priorities of affected people in a coordinated manner, including for SEA, before, 
during and after an emergency.
Participation 
and 
partnership
Adopt agency mechanisms that feed into and support collective/coordinated 
people-centred approaches that enable women, girls, boys, men, including 
the most marginalised and at-risk people among affected communities, to 
participate in and play an active role in decisions that will impact their lives, 
well-being, dignity and protection. Adopt and sustain equitable partnerships 
with local actors to build upon their long-term relationships and trust with 
communities.

In 2022 the IASC Principals released a statement affirming their commitment to AAP as central to 
principled humanitarian action. It pledged to  support humanitarian coordinators, humanitarian country 
teams, clusters and individual agencies in prioritizing the implementation of AAP commitments in all 
humanitarian operations (12). 
In 2023 the IASC Principals approved the IASC collective AAP framework (13) which enables resident/
humanitarian coordinators, humanitarian country teams and UN country teams to prioritize actions to 
strengthen response-wide AAP across six outcome areas (preparedness, needs assessment, planning, 
funding, implementation and monitoring, evaluation and review). WHO must design and implement 
AAP activities in a way that contributes to collective AAP at interagency level. This is discussed more in 
Chapter 8 of this Handbook.
1.3.2 Sphere and the Core Humanitarian Standard
The Sphere handbook (14) health chapter outlines that “in applying the Minimum Standards, all nine 
commitments in the Core Humanitarian Standard should be respected. Feedback mechanisms must 
be put in place during healthcare responses” (pg295). The Core Humanitarian Standard (CHS) on 
quality and accountability (15) promotes “equitable and collaborative relations between people and 
communities and those working to support them. It aims to address power imbalances” (pg2). AAP is 
at the heart of what the CHS aims to achieve.

1.3.3 Grand Bargain
The Grand Bargain 2016 (16) committed donors and humanitarian organi zations to better humanitarian outcomes for 
affected people through enhanced efficiency, effectiveness and greater accountability. 
This included a commitment to a ‘participation revolution’ to include people receiving aid in making decisions which 
affect their lives. Within the overall objective of the Grand Bargain 3.0 (17), endorsed in June 2023, three focus areas are 
envisioned to continue efforts to deliver on the commitments (namely participatory revolution, localization and quality 
funding) with more focused attention on country-level progress. 
1.3.4 Localization
By shifting power and resources to local actors, localization enables affected populations to play a more active role in 
decision-making processes and allows humanitarian actors to draw on local knowledge, expertise and networks. WHO is 
in the process of finalizing a localization strategy to reinforce its principal mission in fragile, conflict-affected, vulnerable 
and protracted emergency settings: strengthening the capacity of national and subnational health authorities to 
prepare for, respond to and prevent health emergencies. This will also support WHO in implementing the Grand Bargain 
commitment (17) to “Provide greater funding and support for the leadership, delivery and capacity of local responders.” 
Achieving a more localized approach to humanitarian action is essential in delivering on AAP . It enables sustainable and 
accountable aid that addresses the needs and respects the values of affected people.

1.3.5 Humanitarian–development–peace nexus
Although this Handbook focuses on WHO health emergencies, it is important to note that affected 
people do not differentiate between humanitarian, development and peace organizations and 
programmes. Participation of communities in decision-making in development and peace programmes 
is as important. It has been ongoing for many years through social accountability approaches and 
participatory rural appraisal, among other approaches. The ideas and principles in this Handbook can 
and should also be integrated in development and peace programmes.
1.4 WHO and AAP 
The values that underpin AAP are strongly reflected in WHO’s constitution (3): “The informed opinion 
and active cooperation on the part of the public are of the utmost importance in the improvement of 
the health of the people.”
These values have continued as central to the way that WHO works, and they feature in core response 
frameworks and approaches.
1.4.1 HEPR framework
This Handbook is aligned with and contributes to the WHO HEPR framework (4), in particular the 
community protection subsystem. This aims to deliver population and environmental health 
interventions intended to manage events in ways that are acceptable, relevant and meaningful to 
those at risk and do not inadvertently create harm. It does this by promoting a community-centred 
approach, harnessing local knowledge and ensuring health strategies are responsive to community 
input and feedback regarding their design, implementation, monitoring and evaluation. 
1.4.2 Risk communication and community engagement
Risk communication is a key approach used by WHO to exchange information between experts and 
people who face risks to their health, to enable them to make informed decisions to mitigate these 
risks. Community engagement is the process of developing relationships with communities to better 
understand their needs and create responsive solutions that are acceptable and workable for affected 
people. This Handbook will support the implementation of this community engagement approach, 
ensuring that we involve communities in decisions that affect them.
1.5 Further reading
WHO competency framework, risk communication and community engagement: for stronger 
and more inclusive health emergency programmes. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2024 
(https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/376653).

Chapter 2 
WHO’s AAP principles
The following principles should underpin all of WHO’s work on AAP .
Safety and dignity 
A ‘do no harm’ approach should be applied to the design and implementation of all programmes and 
AAP components. Risk factors for different groups should be considered, mitigated and monitored 
to make sure that WHO keeps affected people safe. Preserving and promoting the dignity of affected 
people is at the heart of AAP . This is achieved by listening to and responding to their needs and 
allowing their voices, concerns and capacities to be the main drivers of the provision of emergency 
health assistance. 
Confidentiality and data protection 
Confidential treatment of personal and sensitive information received from affected people is an 
important part of staff accountability in the implementation of AAP activities. Personal data should be 
stored securely and in a way that does not put people’s dignity, safety or privacy at risk. Affected people 
need to give informed consent before giving humanitarian responders their personal information. 
Informed consent means they understand why their information is being collected, how it will be used, 
their right to confidentiality and their right to have their data deleted if requested.
Accessibility and non-discrimination
AAP activities should allow for the meaningful inclusion of affected people, in all their diversity, and 
support non-discrimination. This means that factors such as gender, age, disability, sexuality, religion 
and any other diversity factors that are relevant to the context should be considered and planned for 
to ensure that all affected people can provide feedback, participate in decision-making processes and 
benefit from health assistance on an equal footing. 
Gender equality
Gender influences people’s experience of and access to health care. Women and girls often face 
greater barriers than men and boys to accessing health information and services. AAP activities should 
prioritize hearing and responding to the voices of women and girls and designing AAP activities and 
mechanisms that are accessible to them.
Conflict sensitivity
Given that the majority of WHO’s emergency work takes place in fragile, conflict-affected and vulnerable 
settings, and that trust is an essential success factor for any AAP activities, these should be carried out 
in a conflict-sensitive way. This means that programmes are designed and implemented in a way that 
proactively seeks to mitigate the risks of inadvertently exacerbating social tensions, contributing to 
conflict, or undermining factors of social cohesion in each society or community. This is also referred 
to as the ‘do no harm’ principle. 
Prevention and response to sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment (PRSEAH)
Acts of sexual exploitation and abuse (SEA) are the most egregious breaches of accountability by the 
humanitarian community. Staff are required to report SEA by humanitarian workers when it happens, 
and to actively prevent and respond to it. PRSEAH should be considered across the work we do

Chapter 3 AAP in WHO’s emergency response framework
WHO’s Emergency response framework (ERF) edition 2.1 (5) outlines that “WHO’s primary accountability is to the populations it serves, including the principles enshrined in the Accountability 
to Affected Populations commitments.”
In all the critical functions of the ERF, WHO has responsibility for ensuring that emergency responses are accountable to affected people. Table 1 to Table 7:
 • summarize AAP responsibilities across the critical functions;
 • indicate the chapters in this Handbook that provide more information to support the function in fulfilling these; and
 • detail indicators to enable WHE teams at headquarters and regional offices to track the implementation of AAP commitments across emergency response countries through the reflection 
of AAP in standard planning, monitoring and reporting documents.
Annex 5 details indicators that can be used in assessing AAP from the community perspective, and these should be used by country offices to assess AAP impact in country.

Chapter 4 
AAP in the humanitarian 
programme cycle
Affected people, in all their diversity, are involved in and inform all parts of the humanitarian 
programme cycle. 
Why is this important?
The programme cycle is the operational framework that helps ensure humanitarian responses 
remain relevant to, and effective for, the people they serve. AAP principles must be an integral part 
of each stage of the programme cycle to ensure that WHO systems and processes plan, design, 
manage and measure health assistance programmes that respond to the diversity, expressed 
views and rights of affected communities. 
Minimum actions
 • Emergency preparedness activities consider the needs, priorities and rights of affected people 
to effectively prepare for a people-centred response.
 • Situation and needs analysis are people-centred, ensure the views of affected people in all 
their diversity are included, and collect information needed to plan AAP activities.
 • Programme design responds to affected people’s expressed needs and priorities, affected 
people are involved in design decisions and AAP activities are integral to programme design.
 • Programmes are implemented with the participation of affected people and are flexible enough 
to adapt to feedback. 
 • Monitoring includes the collection of qualitative, quantitative and CFM data from affected 
people and involves the participation of affected people.
 • Evaluations use community feedback data on quality and impact of the programme and 
engage affected people in the evaluation process. 
 • Internal systems exist for management to be informed of and take decisions that respond to 
feedback.
 • Internal and external reporting includes data from, and actions taken because of, participation 
and feedback activities.

4.1 Disaster and crisis preparedness
Emergency preparedness planning allows WHO to be able to respond faster and more effectively when 
there is an emergency. AAP should be integrated into preparedness planning in the following ways:
 • Triangulate existing data to inform pre-crisis analysis in the following areas:
 – Understand vulnerabilities and capacities of different groups and who are the most at risk.
 – Understand peace and conflict dynamics and ensure preparedness planning considers, and 
does not unintentionally exacerbate, community tensions.
 – Understand the existing communication channels used by the community as well as their 
information needs, and anticipate how these could be affected by different emergency scenarios.
 – Understand participatory structures and processes that can be activated in an emergency.
 – Map existing CFMs (i.e. collective/interagency mechanisms) that could be scaled up in an 
emergency, or where they do not exist, plan the establishment of a feedback system. 
 • Define how access to health services will be secured for the most vulnerable groups, such as people 
with disabilities, elderly, children, pregnant women, people in remote locations or any other 
vulnerable groups in the country context.
 • Embed activities and approaches across WHO’s AAP commitments in preparedness plans and 
budgets. 
 • Align AAP actions with ministry of health and health cluster preparedness plans.
 • Establish focal persons and clear roles and responsibilities for AAP that can be activated in an 
emergency (see Annex 1 and Annex 2). 
 • Train staff and partners in AAP as a key part of preparedness activities. 
 • Ensure staff, partners and the community know about preparedness plans. 
4.2 Situation analysis and needs/risk assessment
Having a good understanding of the context in which people live is the basis for designing effective 
programmes. It helps us anticipate the evolution of people’s needs as a crisis hits and unfolds. 
WHO and the Global Health Cluster have several public health information approaches and tools 
(20) that feed into understanding and assessing the health situation and needs of a given population 
during an emergency. These tools and approaches must ensure that the views of affected people are 
reflected, and that key information needed to plan AAP activities is collected and reflected. 
4.2.1 PHSA
The PHSA (21) is a key document that highlights emergency- and crisis-related health risks. Based on 
secondary data, it characterizes and quantifies epidemiologic conditions, existing health needs and 
possible health threats faced by the crisis-affected population, including vulnerable and marginalized 
groups. It identifies the major areas for health action to respond to and recover from the crisis at hand 
and identifies major population groups at risk. 
AAP should be reflected in the PHSA in the following ways:
 • As far as possible, use secondary data that reflects participatory approaches and the expressed 
views of affected people, including the most marginalized. 
 • Highlight population-related risks or specificities.
 • Identify pre-existing strategies used to involve communities in health-related decision-making.
 • Identify pre-existing public health communication strategies that could be used to communicate 
AAP and PSEA messages to affected people (see Chapter 6).

• Reflect information on pre-existing CFMs that could be used to enable affected people to reach out 
to WHO with questions, feedback or complaints.
Annex 8 outlines in more detail the AAP information to be included in different sections of the PHSA 
document.
PHSA information that is relevant to the communities should be verified directly with affected people 
to identify gaps or inaccuracies to be updated in the needs assessment. This should be done using 
accessible and inclusive methods as outlined in Chapter 5. 
4.2.2 Health or multisector needs assessment 
Needs assessments fill gaps in or update existing data on the specific needs of affected people, as 
well as provide more specific information to support programme design. The following should be 
considered when planning and implementing needs assessments from an AAP perspective:
 • Coordinate assessments with partners and other sectors to avoid assessment fatigue in 
communities, and ensure effective and collaborative use of existing data.
 • Engage affected people and local partners in designing participatory needs assessments that 
reach the most at-risk people, and that address identified gaps and inaccuracies from the PHSA. 
Communities should also be involved in data interpretation and validation. 
 • During the needs assessment, inform affected people why you are collecting information from 
them, how it will be used and how the results of the needs assessment will be made available to 
them. Do not raise expectations about the level of assistance that will follow the needs assessment.
 • Ensure particularly marginalized groups are adequately considered in needs assessment sampling 
methodology, so that the information collected is representative. 
 • Ensure data collected can be disaggregated by location, gender, age and disability, at a minimum. 
This disaggregation is important in designing adequate programme adaptations for different 
groups. 
 • Design questionnaires to incorporate perceived needs questions, such as in the Humanitarian 
Emergency Settings Perceived Needs Scale (HESPER) (22).
 • Include qualitative data collection methodologies to allow people to express their needs from their 
own perspectives. 
Needs assessments should also assess people’s information and communication needs, preferences 
and barriers to inform the design and delivery of AAP strategies. Key questions to include in needs 
assessments from an AAP perspective are:
 • What are people’s preferred communication channels? 
 • Do people know how to provide feedback or lodge a complaint about programmes or the 
humanitarian response, and how would they prefer to do this? 
 • Are people, in all their diversity, receiving all the information they need to access humanitarian 
assistance? 
 • Are people satisfied with their level of engagement in programme decision-making? What are their 
preferences in terms of participation?
 • Are the people most in need receiving assistance and accessing services? 
 • Are people satisfied with the timeliness, relevance, appropriateness and quality of humanitarian 
assistance? 
 • Are humanitarian actors treating affected people with respect and dignity?
Annex 9 details more example AAP questions to be included in needs assessments.

4.4 Programme design – strategic and 
operational planning
Programme design should address the needs and priorities identified by affected people during needs 
assessments or when registering their opinions through CFMs. Translating their expressed needs into 
concrete action builds and maintains trust with affected communities. 
 • Involve affected people in the design process, so that programmes are co-created or a design is 
checked with them, so it can be adjusted if necessary, especially by and for marginalized groups. 
This will require a flexible approach and being willing to adapt the usual way of doing things. 
 • Ensure the allocation of adequate resources for implementing AAP actions. 
 • Build flexibility into the programme design, as well as into funding proposals and grants contracts, 
in order to respond to monitoring data or feedback from affected people during implementation of 
the programme. 
 • Affected people should feed design decisions into the programme, such as: 
 • identifying the geographical areas most in need; 
 • identifying target groups and designing selection criteria;
 • determining the contents and specification of packages/items for distribution;
 • deciding on the most appropriate timing, frequency and location for activities;
 • prioritizing the most urgent intervention within a limited budget;
 • determining the most suitable adaptations to activities to ensure access of different groups;
 • designing relevant information messages and identifying the best communication channels;
 • planning how you will ensure the regular participation of affected people in decision-making; 
and
 • developing or improving accessible CFMs.

Programme planning documents, such as the WHO emergency operational plan, should describe 
how meaningful consultations have informed design and outline how WHO plans to implement AAP

The humanitarian response plan should include similar information to the above and reflect health

4.5 Emergency response implementation 
Designed activities are delivered, either directly by WHO or by implementing partners. 
 • AAP systems and activities related to participation and inclusion, information provision and 
transparency, and complaints and feedback are implemented. Affected people are actively informed 
of their existence. See chapters 5, 6 and 7 for the specifics of implementing these three areas. 
 • The type of activities implemented will depend on where the country office is on their AAP journey: 
a) taking the first steps, b) putting in place the AAP systems, processes and activities, or c) learning, 
improving and adapting their AAP approach. Annex 11 outlines what activities at these different 
stages look like. 
 • AAP activities should be embedded in emergency operation workplans with responsibilities 
assigned across teams and progress tracked by emergency response leadership. 
 • A specific AAP workplan should be drafted by the AAP focal point. This will break activities down 
into more detail, assign responsibilities across the critical functions and specific teams, and enable 
a closer tracking of progress during implementation. The workplan should touch on all aspects of 
WHO AAP commitments and responsibilities across ERF functions. See Annex 3 for an AAP workplan 
template. 
 • Programme implementation should be done, where possible, with the meaningful participation of 
affected people, including vulnerable and marginalized groups. In the case of medical programme 
delivery, these could be peripheral activities. For example, village health committees have 
responsibilities for the provision of health information, including awareness raising for pregnant 
women on the importance of antenatal care. Community health committees feed into surveillance 
activities. 
4.6 Monitoring 
AAP should be embedded in monitoring processes and tools to track the quality and accountability 
of programmes over time and to identify areas for improvement and course correction. This should 
include process monitoring of beneficiary experiences of humanitarian health programmes as well as 
beneficiary outcome monitoring, whether implemented by WHO or partners. 
4.6.1 Choose indicators to reflect your AAP objectives and plans
 • Include AAP indicators in your operational plan, partnership agreements and donor logframes. 
AAP indicators should cut across all programme areas. Annex 5 includes some suggestions for AAP 
indicators that you can use.
 • Affected people should be involved in designing indicators or choosing the indicators that they feel 
would best describe a successful health intervention from their perspective.

4.6.2 Collect data to measure progress
Data should be collected directly from affected people to produce an accurate understanding of their 
experiences.
 • Involve affected people in designing and implementing monitoring activities.
 • Include questions to monitor AAP in programme monitoring tools used to collect data from affected 
people. 
 • Design new data collection tools, such as patient satisfaction surveys, to better understand affected 
people’s experiences of health assistance. 
 • Include qualitative data collection methods, such as focus group discussions, to allow for the 
exploration of different opinions as well as potential improvements. This should include WHO staff  
going to speak to affected people in the communities they support. 
 • Remember to use data that is already generated through programmes. For example, analysing data 
on the distribution of assistive equipment to people with disabilities could provide insights into 
who has been reached and who has not. Another key example is CFM data, which could show levels 
of satisfaction or dissatisfaction with certain programme components.
 • Include in JORs a review of AAP systems and processes used in country office emergency responses. 
See Annex 10 for questions that can be included in JORs from an AAP perspective. 
4.6.3 Choose what data to collect
Ask questions about: 
 • knowledge and effectiveness of AAP activities including information provision, CFMs and 
participatory processes;
 • people’s experiences of WHO programme activities and any barriers they experience in accessing 
them; and
 • suggestions for improvements in how programmes, or programme components, are delivered.
 • Analyse and reflect on data collected
 • Establish practices for regular analysis and review, together with relevant teams and management, 
to understand progress made and to make programmatic decisions based on the data.
 • Involve affected people in reflecting on and validating monitoring data and feeding into programme 
adaptations.
 • Disaggregate data by location, sex, age and disability, at a minimum, to get an understanding of the 
experiences of different vulnerable groups across locations, and to monitor the effectiveness of any 
adaptations made for particular groups. 
 • Regularly analyse complaints and feedback data and feed it into programme decision-making and 
course correction. 
4.7 Reporting 
Achievements and challenges with implementing AAP activities should be captured and reported. 
4.7.1 Reporting to the community
Where changes to a programme were made based on feedback collected from affected people, 
including complaints and feedback data, this should be documented and shared with affected people. 
Where changes were not made, for example because of contextual challenges, these should also be 
shared. This information could be integrated into community-facing FAQs used by field staff, partners 
and CFMs. See Chapter 6 for more information on communication channels.

4.7.2 WHO reporting
It is important WHO captures and communicates AAP achievements among country offices to support 
sharing of good practice, to track global progress towards IASC and Grand Bargain commitments, and 
to share achievements with Member States and donors. The following should be included in reports:
 • how the needs and concerns of affected people, in all their diversity, have been heard, for example, 
focus group discussions held, satisfaction surveys conducted, or CFMs operating;
 • how many people were involved and some demographic breakdown to show that these activities 
were inclusive;
 • what affected people expressed through the above opportunities, what their major questions, 
concerns or suggestions were, and how these differed by location or vulnerable group;
 • how these questions, concerns or suggestions have been responded to, at an individual level and 
response/programme level; and
 • what adaptations were made in response to the feedback from affected people.
This information should be reflected in the reports being prepared and disseminated by country 
offices, including sitreps, annual country office reports and donor reports.
4.8 Evaluation
Evaluation is a key tool in AAP , as it assesses the extent to which resources at WHO’s disposal were used 
effectively to meet the needs of an affected population. Evaluations provide an opportunity to reflect, 
learn, adapt and improve. The voices and perspectives of affected people are crucial in evaluating the 
outcomes of a humanitarian programme and developing lessons learned, as outlined in the 2023 WHO 
Practical guide to evaluation for programme managers and evaluation staff (23). 
See Annex 10 for questions that can be included in evaluations from an AAP perspective, mapped to 
the evaluation criteria outlined in the WHO Evaluation policy 2018 (24).

Chapter 5  
Participation and inclusion
Affected people, in all their diversity, can meaningfully participate in decisions that affect 
the provision of emergency health assistance.
Why is this important?
Participation enables affected people to take a lead role in identifying and addressing their 
health priorities, promoting a dignified approach that puts them at the centre of humanitarian 
response. In order for the differing and intersecting needs of people to be taken into account, this 
participation should be inclusive of affected people in all their diversity. 
Minimum actions 
 • Affected people are made aware of their right to participate in decisions on humanitarian 
health provision and how they can do this.
 • All affected people can participate equally in identifying and addressing their health priorities.
 • Means of continuous participation across the programme cycle are adapted to ensure 
accessibility for marginalized people, or people with specific needs.
 • Programme staff regularly visit affected communities to understand changing needs and 
concerns.
 • Existing community consultative platforms are used and strengthened, or established where 
these do not exist. 
 • Consultations with affected people are documented, reported into decision-making spaces 
and used to inform programme decisions.
5.1 Understanding existing community 
structures and power relations
It is important to understand the composition of communities, conflict dynamics, existing structures 
for decision-making, and which groups tend to have fewer opportunities to contribute to community 
decision-making. This information can be found from secondary sources as part of a situation analysis. 
Knowing this can help in understanding which voices will be the strongest and which marginalized 
groups WHO needs to seek out to make sure their needs also feed into programmatic decisions – and 
to ensure a conflict-sensitive approach. 
21

================================================================================
Document 32
Source: D:\Fobes Internship\RAG-Project\data\Accountability to Affected People Handbook.pdf
Page: 31
Characters: 3301
================================================================================

5.2 Levels of participation
There are different levels of participation that affected people can have in programmes. The below (25) 
can help in understanding where current programmes are on this scale, and what to aim for. 
 • Inform (e.g. noticeboards): WHO plans and implements programmes according to their 
understanding of needs, informs affected people about plans, but does not provide any opportunity 
to contribute to these plans.
 • Consult (e.g. assessment): WHO asks affected people for their perspectives through surveys or 
discussions and takes this information into account in decision-making, but affected people do not 
have any power to influence the decisions WHO takes.
 • Involve (e.g. community meetings): affected people work with WHO to have an input into 
decisions and provide feedback, but WHO develops the plans and makes the final decisions. 
 • Collaborate (e.g. community committee): affected people and WHO enter a partnership, sharing 
responsibility for decision-making. Where WHO is not able to implement a decision requested by 
affected people, it provides an explanation as to why this is, but WHO still makes the final decisions. 
 • Empower (e.g. community action plan): affected people have complete control over identifying 
problems and developing solutions, as well as guiding the implementation of these. 
Within health programmes, certain elements require highly technical personnel with medical, scientific 
or other qualifications, so it may not be possible to hand over complete control to communities for 
entire programmes. However, there may be elements of programmes where communities can take 
complete control, and these should be assessed and considered.
As outlined in Chapter 4, it is important to ensure that affected people participate in decisions 
across the programme cycle. WHO should aim at a minimum to ‘consult’ with affected people in 
these different processes, but ideally should aim to ‘collaborate’ with them. 
5.3 Structures and opportunities for 
participation
It is important that participation does not become a burden on affected people and, where possible, 
uses existing community structures, such as:
 • Village health committees: where participatory health structures already exist close to 
communities, work with these to feed into different programme decisions. Be aware of how 
representative these committees are of more marginalized groups and plan for the input of those 
that are not represented. 
 • Groups for marginalized or vulnerable persons, such as women, youth or people with 
disabilities: there may be informal structures that can provide advice on accessing more 
marginalized or hidden groups of people. They may have regular meetings that you could ask to 
participate in or attach a consultation session to.
 • Existing participatory structures of health partners: other humanitarian health partners may 
have created participatory structures, such as community committees, to support them with 
ensuring affected people’s involvement in decision-making. Rather than establishing something 
new, WHO could discuss how these structures could be used as a consultative platform for all health 
cluster partners.

If the above structures are not available or additional opportunities are needed, then you can also 
consider:
 • Establishing community committees that are representative of the people WHO is trying to 
reach. These could have responsibility for implementing parts of the programme, for disseminating 
information, or for monitoring programme progress from the community perspective and identifying 
gaps and challenges. 
 • Regular community meetings where many people can attend. This is an opportunity to share 
information, ask and answer questions, and receive feedback and input. 
 • Key informant interviews with representatives of different populations groups or civil society 
organizations to gather different perspectives.
 • Round table meetings with representatives of different population groups to prioritize and agree 
ways forward.
 • Adapting assessment tools/techniques to make sure that the most vulnerable and marginalized 
feel safe and comfortable to contribute their opinions. 
 • Focus group discussions where different groups of people can have less formal conversations and 
express their specific health concerns and challenges. 
 • Working with local civil society organizations which are based within the communities where 
WHO works, and who have a good understanding of specific marginalized groups.
 • WHO staff regularly visiting communities and engaging in informal communication with people 
to gain an up-to-date understanding of challenges and needs within the community. 
5.4 Overcoming organizational challenges to 
participation 
Table 8 suggests solutions for overcoming organizational challenges that can impede participation.
Table 8 Participation: challenges and solutions
Challenge Solutions
Lack of time  • Undertake a rapid consultation process in one day.
 • Identify ongoing activities, monitoring exercises or meetings that could 
be utilized to ask a few additional questions.
 • Speak by phone to community leaders or community-based 
organizations that represent affected people.
 • Use remote digital methods such as SMS or social media. 
 • Use secondary consultative data from other health partners or partners 
from other sectors.
 • Reflect on relevant data from existing CFMs. 
 • Build flexibility into the programme design, so it can be adjusted when 
there is time to undertake consultations with communities.
 • Build time for participation in implementation, monitoring and 
evaluation into the design.

Chapter 6 
Information provision and 
transparency 
Ensure transparent communication with affected people on key programme information 
and respond to their priority information needs, using channels that are equitable, 
appropriate and accessible.
Why is this important?
Receiving accurate information about humanitarian organizations, the assistance they provide 
and affected people’s rights enables affected people to make informed decisions for themselves 
and their families, hold humanitarian actors to account and manage expectations about the 
assistance that can be provided. Providing accurate and up-to-date information can combat 
confusion, mistrust, rumours and misinformation.
Minimum actions
 • Regularly consult with affected people, in all their diversity, to identify their information needs, 
preferred channels and language, and use this information to design information provision 
activities.
 • Share information to affected people on health issues, programme objectives and activities, 
selection criteria, timing and location of services, and their rights and entitlements, including 
their right to provide feedback and make a complaint.
 • Share information on available feedback and complaints channels, their scope and how to use 
them.
 • Inform affected people of the expected standards of conduct by WHO and partner staff, 
including PSEA messaging, and how to report inappropriate actions or behaviours.
 • Adapt information to make it accessible for different groups, including children and people 
with specific needs. 
6.1 Understanding the communication context 
Gain an understanding of what communication systems exist and are readily available to the 
communities WHO is trying to reach. For example, find out if there is reliable mobile infrastructure 
and what percentage of the population have access to mobile phones. Understand if there are 
common ways for sharing and receiving information, such as radio. An AAP working group in country 
may have collected this information, or know where to find it. Alternatively, CDAC Network releases 
Media Landscape Guides for different response countries, which provide significant insights into the 
communication context (see section 6.6).

6.2 Understanding the communication 
preferences and information needs of affected 
people
Needs assessment should include questions to give you a better idea of people’s preferences and 
needs. These questions can be included in WHO needs assessments, or health cluster or multisector 
needs assessments. Annex 9 provides example needs assessment questions related to information 
and communication preferences.
Make sure to collect this needs assessment information from diverse groups in diverse locations to get 
an understanding of differing needs and preferences.
6.3 What information should WHO share?
 • Information about the organization: What is the organization and its partners? How can the 
organization be identified? How can I contact them? What can I expect from the organization and 
its staff?
 • Information about the humanitarian assistance being provided: What assistance is being 
delivered and how can it be used? Where and when is it being delivered? Who is eligible to receive 
assistance and who is not, and why? How do I get in touch if I need more information? Other 
information requested by affected people.
 • Information about affected people’s rights: Right to receive assistance free from any form of 
payment. Right to information about assistance. Right to provide feedback or raise a complaint 
about the assistance. Right to be treated with dignity and respect by aid workers.
Box 1
Information related to the integrity of WHO: protection from sexual exploitation and abuse, 
fraud and corruption 
Making sure that affected people understand the behaviour they should expect from aid workers, 
their right to be treated with dignity and respect, and – if they are not treated in this way – how to 
make a confidential complaint are fundamental ways in which AAP activities support PSEA as well 
as WHO’s efforts to prevent and respond to fraud and corruption.
Country offices should contact PSEA working groups in country for context-specific messaging to 
be used, available materials and advice on how to embed these into different programmes.
6.3.1 Frequently asked questions (FAQ) and answers
A community-focused FAQ document can form the basis of key messaging for affected people. 
Whenever programmes and services are established, change or are coming to an end, the FAQ 
document should be updated to reflect anticipated and actual questions from affected people. 
Staff and partner staff with community-facing roles should be trained on FAQ content. It should also be 
used as part of a CFM to answer questions. It will ensure that information provided to affected people 
about WHO programmes is consistent and accurate.

Box 2
Health Resources and Services Availability Monitoring System (HeRAMS), AAP , and 
information provision and transparency
HeRAMS supports countries with the continuous analysis and dissemination of information on the 
availability of, and accessibility to, essential health resources and services in emergency response 
and fragile states. 
Countries in which HeRAMS is operational should use the information it generates to provide 
affected people with up-to-date information on health service and resource availability. This could 
feed into a collective or WHO health call centre to provide people with up-to-date health referral 
information, or be communicated regularly through some of the other channels mentioned in this 
chapter.
6.4 Effective messaging 
Effective messaging:
 • has a clear goal;
 • is short and simple, and does not contain more information than is needed;
 • is written in the preferred language of the affected community and in multiple languages if needed;
 • uses pictures to convey core messages where possible;
 • uses terminology that has been tested with affected people for comprehension, avoids complex, 
technical language and uses local colloquialisms where appropriate;
 • is coordinated and planned with other health and humanitarian actors to ensure consistency in 
terminology and content across the response; and
 • is delivered respectfully to affected people.
6.5 Communication channels
When choosing which channels to use, consider the following:
 • Use channels that are preferred by affected communities.
 • Use channels that are accessible to marginalized groups, taking into consideration literacy levels, 
visual/auditory impairments, access to technology (e.g. phones and internet), and social/cultural 
barriers.
 • Use a mix of channels, as it is unlikely that one channel will reach everyone, and always provide 
some opportunities for face-to-face communication. 
 • Use face-to-face or phone communication where the message is likely to trigger further questions 
or discussion on individual circumstances.
 • Consider the most appropriate channel for the information to be shared, noting how the choice of 
channel may impact people’s trust in the information. For example, is the information considered 
sensitive, or is the message for each individual or family different?
 • Take advantage of times when there is already face-to-face contact with affected people as part of a 
programme activity to provide additional information.

Chapter 7 
Complaints and feedback
Systematically receive and respond to complaints and feedback from affected people, in all 
their diversity, and adapt programmes according to feedback. 
Why is it important?
Complaints and feedback mechanisms (CFMs) allow humanitarian actors to hear directly from 
affected people to understand their experiences of WHO programmes and enable us to support 
them in navigating and solving their challenges. They provide us with real-time data which 
can alert us to changes in the context, lack of knowledge about programmes, misinformation, 
unexpected oversights in implementation and many more issues.  
Minimum actions 
 • Needs assessments identify accessible and preferred complaint and feedback collection 
mechanisms by consulting with affected people.
 • WHO programmes and targeted communities are covered by a safe, accessible, inclusive CFM 
that ensures confidentiality and data protection.
 • WHO is part of collective CFMs in contexts where these exist, function effectively, and meet the 
needs of affected people that WHO is supporting.
 • Documented processes are in place for complaints handling, referral and response, including 
for sensitive complaints. 
 • Questions, complaints and feedback (including sensitive complaints) from affected people are 
addressed and closed in a timely manner, according to agreed SOPs.
 • Complaints and feedback data is systematically analysed, reported into decision-making 
spaces, and used to inform programme design and course correction.
 • Effectiveness, appropriateness, accessibility of and satisfaction with complaints and feedback 
processes are regularly monitored and used to improve the CFM.
 • Actions taken in response to complaints and feedback from affected communities are reported 
back to them.
7.1 What is a CFM? 
A CFM is a system that is dedicated to receiving, listening to and responding to the questions, views, 
feedback and complaints of affected people on what humanitarian organizations are doing or not 
doing. These could relate to:
 • accessing health services or supplies
 • levels of satisfaction with their experience of health care providers
 • the relevance, quality and fairness of health care provision and supplies
 • the behaviour of staff towards affected people
 • information or misinformation on health issues or services.

7.2 Understanding complaints and feedback 
preferences 
People affected by crisis and conflict may not feel they have the right to voice their opinion or complain. 
They may not feel safe to do so or may think it will have a negative effect on their ability to access 
assistance. It is important to consult with affected people on their preferred way of providing feedback 
or making a complaint, including sensitive complaints. 
Annex 9 provides questions to ask to help assess these preferences. Make sure to consult with different 
segments of the population, who may have different preferences and access barriers.
